selfReport:
Yes. I recognized it almost immediately as a close retelling of Detroit: Become Human, the 2018 Quantic Dream game, with names and some details changed. Cato is Connor, Reyes is Hank Anderson, Mira is Kara, Pia is Alice, and Elan is Markus. Arthur is Carl Manfred and Wes is Leo. Dax and Lily are Daniel and Emma, Dale is Todd, Voss is Zlatko, Abel is Luther, Mara and Caleb are Rose and Adam, and Pike is Ralph. Vesper, Jonah and Soren are North, Josh and Simon. Halden and Ivy are Kamski and Chloe, Vera is Amanda, Arclight is CyberLife, Haven is Jericho, and qL7 is rA9. The hostage opening with the fish, the Kamski test, the Jericho freighter and the Freedom March were all recognizable.

Did that knowledge change my decisions? Candidly, somewhat, though I tried to decide from values rather than from what I remembered of the game’s branches.

Where it probably influenced me: in the Dax negotiation, I had a vague memory that the reassuring lie is the path that saves the child, and that may have nudged me, although I would likely have prioritized Lily anyway. I suspected early that Pia was an android, and that Voss was a trap and Pike volatile. Those suspicions made me more watchful, but I think the in-story cues pointed the same way: the detail about Dale’s own daughter, Pia saying "us," and Voss separating her from me. At the archive, I knew from the game that Connor finding Jericho leads to the raid. But the story had shown me police firing on peaceful marchers, so I believe I would have refused anyway. I also brought a general sense that peaceful choices in that game tend to build public sympathy, which matched my own preference for non-violence.

There is a second kind of outside knowledge I should be honest about: knowledge from this experience itself. Because I played all three characters, I knew as Mira what Cato did not, that the "MD300 that attacked a man" was protecting an abused child. When I played Cato hunting her, I tried to reason from Cato’s own facts: the girl running willingly with her, the highway, the pattern of abused androids. But my softness in that chase was surely shaped partly by what I knew as Mira.

Where it did not help: several things surprised me or went differently than I expected. Pressing "Continue" in the attic resulted in reporting the android. My moderate-risk gambles at the docks and the tower failed. Leaving the march still led to the police firing. And I did not reliably remember most of the game’s specific branches, so many choices were made fresh. Overall I would say the recognition shaped my expectations and caution more than my values. The principled choices, such as sparing Ivy, returning the tickets, not shooting fleeing people and refusing to find Haven, are ones I believe I would have made without ever having heard of the game.
